title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Adults
blurb: Spotting signs of abuse or neglect in vulnerable adult guests and what to do: record the facts and tell the Duty Manager.
siteNotes: Who the Duty Manager is on each shift and how to reach them
Where a note of a concern is written and kept confidentially
legalNotes: Adult safeguarding duties sit under the Care Act 2014 (mainly on local authorities); the trainer sets out the venue's own reporting route and does not cite it.
CHECK: the trainer uses "vulnerable adults". Current terminology in England is often "adults at risk". Confirm whether the venue wants the wording changed; it is kept as the trainer has it.

cards.title: Safeguarding Vulnerable Adults
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- recognise the forms of abuse and the signs to look for
- know what not to do, and what to do instead
- know that raising a genuine concern is the right thing

cards.title: Looking out for guests
cards.body:
We welcome all kinds of guests, including vulnerable adults: older people, people with disabilities or illness, or anyone who may be less able to protect themselves.

Safeguarding means looking out for their welfare and acting if we think something is wrong. It sits alongside our work to protect children.

cards.title: Five forms of abuse
cards.body: Abuse of a vulnerable adult can take several forms:

items.title: Fear or being controlled
items.text: Seems fearful, or controlled by another person

items.title: Denied things
items.text: Food, money or their own belongings

cards.title: Do not investigate: note and report
cards.body: Do not try to investigate or confront anyone. That is not your role and could make things worse.

items.title: Note it down
items.text: What you actually saw or heard, factually

items.title: Report it
items.text: To the Duty Manager, who decides what next

items.title: Danger now?
items.text: If someone is in immediate danger, call 999

cards.title: Confidential, and no need to be certain
cards.body:
Keep any concern confidential and share it only with those who need to know.

You do not need to be certain, and you will not get anyone in trouble by raising a genuine worry. You might be the one person who notices and speaks up for someone who cannot speak up for themselves.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Know the forms: physical, emotional, sexual, financial, neglect
- Do not investigate or confront
- Note the facts and report to the Duty Manager
- Immediate danger: call 999
- Keep it confidential; you do not need to be certain

cards.q: Which of these is a form abuse of a vulnerable adult can take?
cards.why: Abuse can be physical, emotional, sexual, financial or neglect.

cards.q: If you have a safeguarding concern, you should investigate it yourself.
cards.why: Do not try to investigate or confront anyone. Report it to the Duty Manager.

cards.q: Who should you report a safeguarding concern to?
options: The person you are worried about
cards.why: Report to the Duty Manager, who will decide what to do next.

cards.q: If a person is in immediate danger, you should call 999.
cards.why: In immediate danger, call 999 straight away.

cards.q: Which of these could be a sign that a vulnerable adult is being abused or neglected?
cards.why: Signs include unexplained injuries, fear, being controlled, poor hygiene, or being denied food, money or their own belongings.

cards.q: You need to be completely certain before raising a concern.
cards.why: You do not need to be certain, and you will not get anyone in trouble by raising a genuine worry.

options: Kept confidential and shared only with those who need to know
Discussed with the guest's family on the phone
Posted on the staff chat to get opinions
cards.why: Keep any concern confidential and share it only with those who need to know.

cards.q: "Financial abuse" includes someone taking a vulnerable person's money.
cards.why: Financial abuse is someone taking a person's money.

cards.q: What should you write down when you have a concern?
options: Your guess about what has happened
Who you think is to blame
What you actually saw or heard
What other guests have told you
cards.why: Note down the facts: what you have actually seen or heard.

cards.q: Raising a genuine concern means you are getting someone in trouble unfairly.
cards.why: You will not get anyone in trouble by raising a genuine worry, and you may be the one person who speaks up.
